transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Hi, doctor. Thank you for seeing me. Well, I guess I'm here because... you know, I've been really struggling lately with my evenings. I'm an insurance sales agent, so I spend all day on the phone, sitting at a desk, dealing with clients, and I really, really try to be so careful about what I eat during the day. I'll just have a small salad or a piece of fruit, just trying to be good and keep things under control, you know? 

But then I get home. And some evenings after work, especially on the days where I've been incredibly strict with myself all day long, it just sort of... falls apart. I'll walk in the door, put my bag down, and I tell myself I'm just going to have a normal, sensible dinner. But I end up eating way, way more than I ever meant to. It's like I just lose track of everything. I'll have my dinner, but then I'm still standing there in the kitchen, so I'll pour a huge bowl of cereal. And then I'm eating crackers right out of the box while I'm putting the milk away. Then I'll find some leftovers in the fridge—maybe some cold pasta or whatever is in there—and I'll eat that too. And then, of course, I need something sweet, so I'm digging into whatever sweets or cookies I have in the pantry. And it's just... before I even realize what's happening, I've eaten all of this food, just a huge amount, all within a couple of hours. I just keep doing it, and it's really starting to upset me, which is why I finally decided I needed to come in and talk to somebody about it.
After these episodes of eating a large amount of food in the evening, do you ever try to compensate for it by making yourself vomit, using laxatives, or exercising excessively?

Oh, no, no, I don't do the throwing up thing. And definitely no laxatives, that just sounds awful and honestly, I wouldn't even know how to hide something like that. But... I definitely feel this intense, overwhelming need to fix it, you know? Like I have to somehow undo the damage of all those crackers and cereal and everything else I just shoved in my face the night before. 

So, the next morning, I wake up feeling just so heavy and disgusted with myself, and I'll tell myself, "Okay, that's it, you are making up for this today." So I will completely skip breakfast. I won't even look at food. And then I'll skip lunch too, just drinking black coffee at my desk while I'm making my insurance calls, completely ignoring my stomach growling because I feel like I deserve to be hungry after what I did. 

And then... yeah, you mentioned exercise, and I guess I do push that pretty hard to compensate. Like, on the weekends, if I had a bad Friday night, I'll force myself to go on an extra-long hike. There's this trail near my house that usually takes maybe forty-five minutes, but I'll make myself do the steep three-hour loop, even if my knees are aching and I'd rather be resting. Or during the week, I play in this women's softball league—well, I say recreational, but we have actual conditioning drills—and if I've had one of my bad eating nights, I will push myself so, so hard during those drills. I'll just keep running and pushing myself to the limit, even when I'm already completely exhausted from working all day and barely eating anything. It's just this constant need to try and burn off the guilt, because if I don't skip those meals or push myself like that, I just sit there obsessing over everything I ate.
During these times when you're eating a lot in the evening, do you feel like you can't stop eating or control how much you're eating, even if you wanted to?

Yes, that is exactly it. It's honestly the scariest part of the whole thing. Because I do want to stop, I really, really do. I'll be standing there, looking at the empty cereal bowl or the cracker box, and in my head, I'm literally screaming at myself, "Okay, that's enough, you had your dinner, you had your snack, just go sit down in the living room." 

And I'll even try! I'll walk out of the kitchen, I'll go sit on the couch, I'll pick up the TV remote and try to find a show to distract myself. But my brain is just... it's like it's been completely hijacked. I can't even focus on the screen. The next thing I know, I'm getting right back up, walking back into the kitchen, opening the pantry door all over again. I'll tell myself, "Just one more cookie," but then I'm eating three or four. And I just keep doing that. Once I get started on those nights, it's like I keep going back to the kitchen even while I'm actively telling myself to stop. My hands are just moving on their own, opening bags and containers, and it's like I'm completely disconnected from the steering wheel. 

I don't really feel like I'm back in charge of my own body until I hit this point where I'm just so uncomfortably full. Like, my stomach will be stretched tight, and it almost physically hurts to swallow another bite. Only then does the spell kind of break, you know? And then I'm just left standing there in the middle of the kitchen, surrounded by crumbs and wrappers, feeling absolutely horrible about myself and wondering how I let it happen again when I promised myself that morning I wouldn't. It's just this awful, out-of-body feeling where my willpower just evaporates completely, no matter how hard I try to hold onto it.
On average, how often do these episodes of eating a large amount of food in the evening happen?

Well, if I really sit down and look at how things have been going—which I try not to do too much because it just makes me feel so guilty—but if I'm being completely honest, for the past few months, this has been happening most weeks. I'd say it's usually one or two nights a week where I just completely go off the rails and eat far, far more than I ever planned to. 

Like, it might be a Tuesday, because Tuesdays are always my heaviest days for policy renewals and I'm just on the phone dealing with frustrated clients all day long. So I come home completely drained, and then it happens. I'll eat all that food, just a mountain of it, like I described before. And then the very next day, Wednesday, I wake up and I just have to try and make up for it. So I'll be right back to skipping my meals, just sitting at my desk drinking my black coffee and ignoring my stomach, or I'll make sure I'm exercising longer than usual that evening to try and burn it all off. 

It's just this constant, exhausting cycle, you know? One or two bad nights of eating, followed immediately by a day of starving myself or pushing myself to the absolute limit on a hike or at softball just to fix what I did. And it’s been exactly like that, week in and week out, for months now. I keep telling myself at the start of every week, "Okay, this week is going to be different, you're just going to eat normally every night," but then Thursday rolls around, I'm stressed out, and the whole thing just starts all over again.
Can you tell me more about the feeling of not being able to stop eating during these episodes? Does it feel like you're completely unable to control yourself once you start, even if you wanted to?

Yeah, I think... I know I touched on this a minute ago, but it's just so hard to explain because it doesn't make sense even to me. But yes, it's exactly like that. It's like I'm completely unable to control myself. I mean, I'll be standing there, and I know I shouldn't be eating more. I know it. My brain is saying, "You're not even hungry anymore, what are you doing?" But my body is just doing it anyway. 

It's like... once I get started on those nights, it's like I keep going back to the kitchen even while I'm telling myself to stop. I'll walk away, like I said, I'll try to go watch TV or maybe check my emails for work—because there's always some client complaining about their premium going up, you know how it is—but I can't even read the words on the screen. My mind is just completely fixated on the pantry. And then I'm just up and walking back in there. I'll open the cabinet, grab another handful of whatever, maybe some chips or those little chocolate candies I keep telling myself I'm going to throw away but never do. 

And it's just this awful feeling of being a passenger in my own body. I'm watching myself do it, and I'm feeling so much shame, but I can't put the brakes on. I don't really feel back in charge until I'm uncomfortably full. Like, physically, painfully full, where I just have to sit down and hold my stomach because it's stretched so tight. That's the only thing that stops me. It's not my willpower, it's not me deciding to stop. It's just my body physically not being able to take one more bite. And then the guilt just washes over me, and it's so heavy, just thinking about how I let it happen again when I was trying so hard not to.
Can you tell me if, during these episodes, you feel a complete lack of control over how much you're eating—like you're unable to stop even though you want to?

I know we keep circling back to this, and I feel like a broken record, but yes—a hundred percent yes. It is a complete and total lack of control. I really meant what I was trying to explain just a minute ago. 

It’s... it’s so frustrating because I’m a fifty-year-old woman, you know? I manage complicated insurance policies all day, I deal with difficult clients, I handle my life. I should be able to manage my own dinner. But then I get home, and once I get started on those bad nights, it's like I just keep going back to the kitchen, over and over again, even while I'm actively telling myself to stop. I'll literally be whispering to myself, "Don't do it, don't open the fridge," but my hand is already on the handle. It's like my brain and my body are two completely different entities at that point. 

I can want to stop more than anything in the world, but I just can't make myself do it. And like I said, I don't really feel like I'm back in charge of myself until I am just so uncomfortably full. It takes that physical discomfort, that feeling of my stomach being stretched so tight I can barely breathe, for the spell to finally break. Until my body forces me to stop because there's simply no room left, I have zero control over how much I'm having. None whatsoever. It's just... it's exhausting to live with, to be completely honest with you.

Can you confirm if these episodes of not being able to control your eating happen specifically during a defined time, like the couple of hours after you get home in the evening, rather than being spread out throughout the day or happening multiple times a day?

Yes, exactly. It’s not an all-day thing at all. I mean, during the day, I’m actually incredibly strict with myself. I’m at the office, I’m dealing with all those insurance policies and putting out fires, so I’m busy and I can just power through on black coffee and sheer willpower. I keep a very tight lid on things from the minute my alarm goes off until I finally leave the office. So no, it’s definitely not spread out or happening multiple times throughout the day. 

But what actually brought me in, the whole reason I realized I really needed to talk to someone about this, is exactly what happens in that specific window after work. It’s always the evenings. I’ll walk through the front door, and especially on those days where I’ve been so, so strict all day long, it’s like a dam just breaks. The whole episode, all of that eating I was just describing, it all happens within just a couple of hours. 

I’ll start by just having my dinner, you know, telling myself I’m just going to sit down and have a normal, sensible meal to unwind. But then... then I just end up eating way, way more than I ever meant to. Within that short little window, maybe a two-hour block right after I get home, I’ll finish my dinner and then immediately go back to the kitchen and pour myself a bowl of cereal. And then probably another one. And then I’m opening a sleeve of crackers, just eating them dry right out of the box while I stand there. Then I’ll start digging around for leftovers in the fridge—like cold pasta or whatever is sitting in Tupperware from two nights ago—and I’ll eat all of that, too. And then, of course, the craving shifts and I have to have sweets, so I’m hunting down chocolate or cookies or whatever I can find. 

All of that food, just crammed into those couple of hours right after I get home. Once that evening window is over and I’m just too physically stuffed to move, it stops. But it’s always that specific, defined time when I’ve finally let my guard down after being so disciplined all day.
Are there times when you experience these episodes of eating a large amount of food in the evening without using compensatory behaviors like skipping meals or overexercising the next day?

No, I don't think there's ever a time where I just... let it go. I wish I could, I really do, because it would be so much easier to just wake up and say, "Okay, today is a new day, let's just move on." But my mind just doesn't work like that. The guilt is just so overwhelming when my alarm goes off. I'll lay there in bed, feeling how bloated and heavy my stomach still is from the night before, and immediately the math starts in my head. I have to fix it. I have to undo what I just did. 

So, no, I always have to do something. The next day after one of those nights, I'll tell myself I'm making up for it by completely skipping breakfast and lunch. I know I mentioned I'm already pretty strict during the day, but after a bad night, it's different—it's like a punishment. I won't let myself have a single bite at the office, no matter how much my stomach starts growling around noon or if one of the other agents brings in bagels for the breakroom. I just drink my black coffee and tell myself I don't deserve to eat after what I did the night before. 

And it's not just skipping meals, either. I physically make myself pay for it. I'll force myself to go take an extra-long hike on the trails behind my subdivision, going way further than I normally would, just trying to sweat it out. Or... well, I play in this recreational softball league. It's usually just for fun, you know, a bunch of us older ladies trying to stay active and get away from our desks. But if we have conditioning practice the day after an episode, I will push myself so much harder than anyone else out there. I'll run drills until my lungs are absolutely burning, even when I'm already completely exhausted and just dead tired from not eating all day. I just feel this intense, overwhelming need to burn off every single mistake I made the night before. So, to answer your question, no, I can't just have one of those episodes and move on. I'm always trying to balance the scales the next day.
Do these episodes of eating a large amount of food in the evening usually happen when you're alone, or do they often occur in the presence of other people?

You know, I haven't really stopped to think about that. I guess I'm just not sure. I mean, when I get into that state, my mind is so laser-focused on the food and that overwhelming urge I was telling you about, that I don't really pay attention to whether the house is empty or not. 

My husband, he works a lot of evenings—he manages a hardware store over on Route 9 and they do inventory on Tuesdays and Thursdays, plus he's in a bowling league on Wednesdays with some of the guys from his old high school. So sometimes he's out of the house completely. But other times, he's right there in the living room, sitting in his recliner watching his history documentaries with the volume turned way up because he absolutely refuses to get his hearing checked, no matter how many times I nag him about it. 

So he could be in the very next room while I'm in the kitchen, or he could be halfway across town, and I don't think it really changes anything for me. I just... I get home from the agency, I put my keys in the bowl, take off my work shoes—which is a whole production because my feet are always swelling up by the end of the day from running around the office and standing at the filing cabinets—and the urge just hits me. Once that dam breaks, like I said earlier, I'm just in the kitchen eating. 

So I really couldn't tell you if it's mostly when I'm alone or when people are there. I just haven't noticed a pattern with that at all. It's really just that specific time of day that triggers it, regardless of who happens to be around.
Do these episodes of not being able to control your eating cause you a lot of emotional distress or upset?

Emotional distress? I... gosh, I'm really not sure how to answer that. I mean, what exactly do you mean by emotional distress? Because, well, my whole life is pretty stressful, to be perfectly honest with you, so it's hard to separate it all out. 

Working in insurance, especially at my age when you're dealing with these young kids coming into the agency who think they know everything because they took a weekend online seminar, but they can't even fill out a basic liability form without my help... it's just exhausting. I'm constantly hovering over their desks, putting out their fires, dealing with angry clients on the phone. And then I come home, and like I said, the dam just breaks and I start eating. 

But am I emotionally distressed about the eating itself? I haven't really noticed feeling that way. I don't think I sit there crying or feeling, you know, devastated or having a breakdown over it. I'm just kind of on autopilot. I know I mentioned the guilt the next morning, and needing to fix it by skipping meals or running myself ragged on the trails, but as far as the episodes themselves actually causing me a lot of emotional upset... I just don't know. 

I've never really stopped to take my emotional temperature, I guess you could say. I'm so used to just keeping my head down and powering through everything life throws at me. Like when my husband had his knee surgery last year—I was working full time, taking care of him, managing the house, doing all the driving, and I never once broke down or got upset. I just do what needs to be done. So with the food... I don't know. I haven't really noticed feeling distressed. I just do it, and then I do what I have to do the next day to make up for it. So I really couldn't say for sure if it causes me emotional distress, because I don't even know what that would look like for me at this point.
Do you feel upset, ashamed, or distressed specifically about the fact that you eat such large amounts during these evening episodes?

Well, like I was just saying... I'm really not sure. I mean, "upset, ashamed, distressed"—those are very big words, aren't they? They feel so heavy. And honestly, I don't know if I can say yes to that. I just haven't really noticed feeling that specific way about the amount I'm eating. 

I know you're asking specifically about the large amounts, but... I don't know, it's just what happens. Like I said, I come home, my feet are throbbing, I'm exhausted from dealing with the new kids at the agency who can't even tell a premium from a deductible, and I just start eating. I don't sit there at the kitchen counter looking at the empty wrappers or the empty boxes and think, "Oh, I'm so ashamed of how much this is." I really don't. 

I mean, maybe I should? Maybe normal people would look at all that and feel distressed right then and there. But I just... I don't. I'm just eating. The shame, or whatever you want to call it, only really hits me the next morning when I wake up and feel my stomach, like I told you before. That's when I feel like I need to fix it. But about the actual fact that I'm eating so much in the moment? Or even right after? I haven't really stopped to analyze it like that. 

I'm just a very pragmatic person, I suppose. I don't spend a lot of time wallowing in my feelings. Even when my mother passed away—bless her heart, she was 82 and it was her time, but still—I didn't sit around crying for weeks. I planned the funeral, I sorted out her estate, I dealt with the probate court because my sister certainly wasn't going to do it... I just handled it. So with this, I just don't know if I feel distressed about the amounts. I just do it, and then the next day I deal with the consequences. So, no, I can't really say I've noticed feeling upset or ashamed specifically about how much I'm eating. I just haven't.
During these evenings when you're eating a lot, do you ever feel like you're not in control of yourself at all, like your actions are automatic or happening without your full awareness?

You know, when you put it exactly like that... yes. Yes, I do. It's the strangest feeling, really, because like I was just saying, I'm a very pragmatic, organized person. At the agency, I'm the one steering the ship, making sure the new kids don't accidentally cancel someone's comprehensive auto policy or mess up a premium calculation. I make hundreds of decisions a day, and I am always in the driver's seat. 

But then I get home, and... it's like someone else just takes the wheel. Once I get started on those nights, it's just... I can't seem to put the brakes on. I'll be in the kitchen, and I'll eat something—maybe a bowl of cereal or some leftover casserole—and then I'll walk into the living room. And in my head, my logical brain is telling myself, "Okay, that's enough, you're done now. You've had your snack." I am literally telling myself to stop. 

But then, it's like my body isn't listening to my brain. I just keep going back to the kitchen. I'll sit down for two minutes, and then I'm right back up, opening the pantry, grabbing a box of crackers or cookies, whatever is sitting there. It really does feel automatic, like you said. It's like my hands are just moving on their own, opening wrappers and putting food in my mouth, while the sensible part of me is just watching it happen, shouting at me to cut it out. 

And honestly, I don't really feel like I'm back in charge of myself until I hit this wall where I'm just uncomfortably full. Like, physically stretched to the absolute limit where my stomach is aching and I have to unbutton my work trousers just to sit there and breathe properly. That physical discomfort is usually the only thing that finally snaps me out of that... that trance, or whatever you want to call it. Up until that point where I physically can't fit anything else in, the whole thing just happens without me really consenting to it, if that makes any sense.
Do you feel a strong dislike for your body shape or weight, or does the way you see your body cause you significant distress?

Well, "distress" is another one of those heavy words, but... I suppose, yes, it does bother me quite a bit, but mostly in how it affects my professional life. You have to understand, in the insurance business, presentation really is everything. You're selling trust, you're selling a promise. When I started in this industry right out of high school, we wore these very structured suits, and you had to look impeccable. It's a bit more business casual now, but I still firmly believe in looking sharp, especially when I have to go to these regional leadership meetings or when I'm taking a big commercial client out to lunch.

And that's where my shape and my weight really start to mess with my head. If I'm getting dressed in the morning before a client luncheon or a leadership meeting, and my waistband feels tight? It just... it completely ruins my day. I'll be standing there tugging at my trousers, trying to pull my blazer down just right to cover my stomach, and I just start feeling like I look entirely sloppy. It's this awful, sinking feeling. I get so worried that people won't take me as seriously, like they'll look at me and think, "Well, if she can't even manage her own waistline, how is she going to manage my commercial liability policy?" 

And the most frustrating part of it all is that I *know* I'm good at what I do. I know I've still been doing my job, and doing it better than half the people in that office! I'm the one keeping the agency afloat when the new kids make a mess of things. My numbers are rock solid. But the second I feel that tight waistband digging into me, all that logical confidence just evaporates. I'll spend the whole luncheon sitting up rigidly, holding my breath, just agonizing over how heavy and unprofessional I must look to everyone else across the table. I can barely even focus on what the client is saying because I'm so hyper-aware of how my clothes are fitting. So, yes, I suppose you could say it causes me a significant amount of distress, because I just can't let it go when I feel like my body is making me look like I don't know what I'm doing.

Do these concerns about your body shape or weight only come up after these evening eating episodes, or do you feel this way about your body most of the time, even when you haven't had one of those nights?

Well, I... I'm really not sure how to answer that, to be perfectly honest with you. I haven't exactly sat down and charted it out or kept a diary of when I feel bad about my waistline versus when I've had one of those nights in the kitchen. I mean, who has the time for that? Between managing the agency, dealing with the underwriters, and trying to keep the new hires from completely sinking our quarterly numbers, my days just sort of blur together into one long sprint. 

So, if you're asking if it's only after I eat all that food, or if it's every single day... I just don't know. I haven't really separated the two in my head. Like I was saying before about getting dressed for those client luncheons or leadership meetings—when I'm standing there in front of the mirror, tugging at my blazer and worrying that I look sloppy, I'm not really stopping to think, "Oh, is this because of what I ate last night, or is this just how I feel in general?" I'm just in a panic about looking unprofessional in the moment. 

And really, my mornings are so incredibly rushed anyway. I have to be up at the crack of dawn because the regional managers are on East Coast time, so they're sending emails while I'm still trying to get my coffee brewed. By the time I'm actually putting my work trousers on, my mind is already running through a checklist of ten different commercial liability policies that need reviewing before nine o'clock. So if the trousers feel tight, I just get that awful, sinking feeling I told you about, but I honestly couldn't tell you if it's a daily occurrence or if it's strictly tied to those specific evenings when I lose control in the pantry. I just haven't paid that kind of focused attention to the timing of it all, I suppose. It just happens when it happens, and I have to deal with it and get out the door.
Do you feel dissatisfied with your body shape or weight on most days, even when you haven’t had one of these evening eating episodes?

Well, if I really sit here and try to parse it out the way you're asking... I suppose it's not necessarily a constant, every-single-minute kind of thing on a random Tuesday when I'm just buried in paperwork at my desk. But I know I keep coming back to this—it really hits me the hardest on the days that matter most, regardless of whether I was up late in the kitchen the night before or not. 

It all really comes down to how my clothes are fitting when I have to be the face of the agency. Like I was saying earlier, if my waistband feels tight before a client luncheon or one of those big leadership meetings, that's when it just completely consumes me. I instantly start feeling like I look terribly sloppy, and I get so fixated on the idea that people won't take me as seriously. 

And it is just infuriating, honestly, because in my logical mind, I know I've still been doing my job! I could have just closed a massive commercial fleet policy the day before, perfectly executed, catching errors that the underwriters completely missed, but if I'm standing in the mirror and that skirt is digging into my sides, all that professional pride just vanishes. I start obsessing over whether the client is judging my waistline instead of listening to my liability presentation. It's like my brain completely disconnects my actual competence from my physical appearance. 

So, even if I haven't had one of those eating episodes, if the clothes don't fit right on a day I need to be at the top of my game... yes, that awful dissatisfaction is absolutely there. It just takes over, no matter how well I know I'm running that office.
Do you find yourself thinking about your body shape or weight in a negative way on most days, even when you haven't had one of these episodes the night before?

Well, like I was just trying to explain... I feel like we're covering the same ground here, Doctor, but yes, absolutely. It really doesn't matter if I had an episode the night before or if I just went to bed early after watching the evening news. If it's a day where I have a client luncheon on the schedule, or one of those big regional leadership meetings, and I go to put on my work trousers or my skirt and that waistband feels tight... it just completely derails me. 

I immediately start feeling like I look entirely sloppy. And in the insurance business, sloppy is practically a death sentence for your credibility. I just get this overwhelming, nagging dread that people won't take me seriously, that they'll look at my waistline and think I'm losing my edge or that I can't manage my own life, let alone their liability coverage. 

And it makes me so incredibly angry with myself because, as I keep saying, I know I've still been doing my job! I'm the one carrying that office. I'm the one keeping the complex commercial accounts in perfect order while the younger agents are busy checking their phones and making careless data entry errors. I know my actual work is impeccable. I have the numbers to prove it. But none of that logical proof seems to matter in my head if my clothes are digging into my sides. I just can't shake that negative feeling about my body, episode or no episode. It just hangs over me the entire day, and I can't stop thinking about it.
Do you find yourself feeling dissatisfied with your body shape or weight on days when you have not had one of these evening eating episodes?

Doctor, I... I feel like we are just going in circles here. I really do. I mean, I've answered this, haven't I? But yes, to be perfectly, abundantly clear—yes. If I wake up on a Thursday, say, and I haven't had one of those terrible nights in the pantry on Wednesday, but I have a major client luncheon on the books... if I go to put on my navy suit, the one I usually wear for the big commercial fleet accounts, and that waistband is digging into my stomach? It completely ruins me. 

I don't know how else to explain it other than it just takes over my entire thought process. I stand there in the mirror, and I just see this sloppy, unkempt person looking back at me. And in my line of work, you simply cannot look sloppy. You just can't. If I walk into a leadership meeting looking like I can't even manage my own waistline, how on earth are these regional directors going to trust me to manage millions of dollars in liability coverage? They won't. They'll just look at me and think I'm losing my grip. 

And that's what makes it so maddening! Because, as I've said, I *know* I'm doing my job. I know I am. I'm the one catching the mistakes the underwriters make. I'm the one keeping the agency afloat while half the staff is scrolling on their phones. I have the competence, I have the track record, but the second my clothes feel tight, all of that just evaporates from my mind. I just feel awful about my body, and it doesn't matter one bit if I had an episode the night before or not. The dissatisfaction is just... it's just there, and it's loud, and it makes me feel like a complete fraud, regardless of my actual professional capabilities.
Do you judge or evaluate yourself negatively based on your body shape or weight, even on days when you haven’t had one of these evening eating episodes?

Doctor, I am really trying my best to be patient here, but I honestly feel like I am repeating myself for the fourth time. Yes. Yes, I do judge myself negatively. I evaluate myself entirely on that basis, and as I have explained in great detail, it has absolutely nothing to do with whether I was up late eating the night before. 

It is exactly what I have been saying: if I have a client luncheon—say, with one of the big contractors we cover—or if I have to sit in a leadership meeting with the regional vice presidents, and my waistband feels tight... that is it. That is the moment the judgment starts. I look in the mirror and I just think, "You look sloppy. You look like a mess." And the immediate leap my brain makes is that everyone else in that room is going to think the exact same thing. I get so caught up in this belief that they won't take me seriously. I sit there at the head of the conference table, and instead of focusing on the liability limits I'm presenting, I'm just agonizing over whether they are staring at my stomach and thinking I'm incapable. 

And it is just so incredibly frustrating—which I feel like I've made clear—because I *know* I have been doing my job! I know my work is flawless. I know I am the one keeping that agency running while the younger agents are making careless mistakes left and right. But all of that professional worth, all of my actual competence... it just goes right out the window the second my clothes don't fit right. So yes, to answer your question yet again, I absolutely evaluate myself negatively based on my shape, and it happens whether I had an episode or not.

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if I feel like I'm not in control of myself or if my actions are automatic during the eating episodes, which directly maps to the Loss of Control symptom.

patient.answer:
You know, when you put it exactly like that... yes. Yes, I do. It's the strangest feeling, really, because like I was just saying, I'm a very pragmatic, organized person. At the agency, I'm the one steering the ship, making sure the new kids don't accidentally cancel someone's comprehensive auto policy or mess up a premium calculation. I make hundreds of decisions a day, and I am always in the driver's seat. 

But then I get home, and... it's like someone else just takes the wheel. Once I get started on those nights, it's just... I can't seem to put the brakes on. I'll be in the kitchen, and I'll eat something—maybe a bowl of cereal or some leftover casserole—and then I'll walk into the living room. And in my head, my logical brain is telling myself, "Okay, that's enough, you're done now. You've had your snack." I am literally telling myself to stop. 

But then, it's like my body isn't listening to my brain. I just keep going back to the kitchen. I'll sit down for two minutes, and then I'm right back up, opening the pantry, grabbing a box of crackers or cookies, whatever is sitting there. It really does feel automatic, like you said. It's like my hands are just moving on their own, opening wrappers and putting food in my mouth, while the sensible part of me is just watching it happen, shouting at me to cut it out. 

And honestly, I don't really feel like I'm back in charge of myself until I hit this wall where I'm just uncomfortably full. Like, physically stretched to the absolute limit where my stomach is aching and I have to unbutton my work trousers just to sit there and breathe properly. That physical discomfort is usually the only thing that finally snaps me out of that... that trance, or whatever you want to call it. Up until that point where I physically can't fit anything else in, the whole thing just happens without me really consenting to it, if that makes any sense.

target_item.name: Body_Image_Weight_Shape_Disturbance

patient.answer:
Well, "distress" is another one of those heavy words, but... I suppose, yes, it does bother me quite a bit, but mostly in how it affects my professional life. You have to understand, in the insurance business, presentation really is everything. You're selling trust, you're selling a promise. When I started in this industry right out of high school, we wore these very structured suits, and you had to look impeccable. It's a bit more business casual now, but I still firmly believe in looking sharp, especially when I have to go to these regional leadership meetings or when I'm taking a big commercial client out to lunch.

And that's where my shape and my weight really start to mess with my head. If I'm getting dressed in the morning before a client luncheon or a leadership meeting, and my waistband feels tight? It just... it completely ruins my day. I'll be standing there tugging at my trousers, trying to pull my blazer down just right to cover my stomach, and I just start feeling like I look entirely sloppy. It's this awful, sinking feeling. I get so worried that people won't take me as seriously, like they'll look at me and think, "Well, if she can't even manage her own waistline, how is she going to manage my commercial liability policy?" 

And the most frustrating part of it all is that I *know* I'm good at what I do. I know I've still been doing my job, and doing it better than half the people in that office! I'm the one keeping the agency afloat when the new kids make a mess of things. My numbers are rock solid. But the second I feel that tight waistband digging into me, all that logical confidence just evaporates. I'll spend the whole luncheon sitting up rigidly, holding my breath, just agonizing over how heavy and unprofessional I must look to everyone else across the table. I can barely even focus on what the client is saying because I'm so hyper-aware of how my clothes are fitting. So, yes, I suppose you could say it causes me a significant amount of distress, because I just can't let it go when I feel like my body is making me look like I don't know what I'm doing.

patient.answer:
Well, I... I'm really not sure how to answer that, to be perfectly honest with you. I haven't exactly sat down and charted it out or kept a diary of when I feel bad about my waistline versus when I've had one of those nights in the kitchen. I mean, who has the time for that? Between managing the agency, dealing with the underwriters, and trying to keep the new hires from completely sinking our quarterly numbers, my days just sort of blur together into one long sprint. 

So, if you're asking if it's only after I eat all that food, or if it's every single day... I just don't know. I haven't really separated the two in my head. Like I was saying before about getting dressed for those client luncheons or leadership meetings—when I'm standing there in front of the mirror, tugging at my blazer and worrying that I look sloppy, I'm not really stopping to think, "Oh, is this because of what I ate last night, or is this just how I feel in general?" I'm just in a panic about looking unprofessional in the moment. 

And really, my mornings are so incredibly rushed anyway. I have to be up at the crack of dawn because the regional managers are on East Coast time, so they're sending emails while I'm still trying to get my coffee brewed. By the time I'm actually putting my work trousers on, my mind is already running through a checklist of ten different commercial liability policies that need reviewing before nine o'clock. So if the trousers feel tight, I just get that awful, sinking feeling I told you about, but I honestly couldn't tell you if it's a daily occurrence or if it's strictly tied to those specific evenings when I lose control in the pantry. I just haven't paid that kind of focused attention to the timing of it all, I suppose. It just happens when it happens, and I have to deal with it and get out the door.

inference.note: The patient continues to describe episodes of loss of control eating in the evening, followed by compensatory behaviors such as fasting and excessive exercise.
